script: I think the bus is better than the car for short trips in town. It costs less. You do not have to look for a parking space. And you can read on the way. The only problem is the evening, when buses come every half hour.

items.stem: Why does the writer prefer the bus?
items.rationale: The writer gives cost, no parking search and being able to read; none of the other options is mentioned as a reason.

items.stem: What does the writer say is a problem?
options: Buses are rare in the evening
Buses do not stop in town
items.rationale: The last sentence names the evening as the only problem, when buses come every half hour.

items.stem: What kind of trips is the writer talking about?
items.rationale: The first sentence limits the comparison to short trips in town.

script: Our office should keep the plants in the meeting room. Some people say they take too much time. But watering them takes five minutes a week. The room is nicer with them, and two visitors have said so this month.

items.stem: What does the writer want?
items.rationale: The first sentence states the position: the plants in the meeting room should stay.

items.stem: What is the argument against the plants?
items.rationale: The writer reports that some people say the plants take too much time, then answers that objection.

items.stem: What evidence does the writer give?
items.rationale: The writer says two visitors have said the room is nicer this month.

script: I do not agree that we need a new printer. The old one still works. It is slow, but we only print about ten pages a day now. A new printer costs six hundred dollars. We could spend that money on the broken chairs instead.

items.stem: What is the writer's opinion?
options: A new printer is not needed
A new printer should be bought
The old printer should be repaired
items.rationale: The opening sentence disagrees with the need for a new printer and the rest supports that.

items.stem: What does the writer admit about the old printer?
items.rationale: The writer concedes that it is slow, then argues that ten pages a day makes this unimportant.

items.stem: What does the writer suggest instead?
items.rationale: The final sentence proposes spending the money on the broken chairs.

script: The gym should open at six in the morning, not seven. Many members start work at eight. One hour is not enough time to train, wash and travel. The staff say six is too early, but two other gyms in this town already open then.

items.stem: What does the writer ask for?
items.rationale: The writer asks the gym to open at six rather than seven.

items.stem: Why is seven o'clock a problem?
options: There is not enough time before work
The gym is too busy then
items.rationale: Members who start work at eight cannot train, wash and travel in one hour.

items.stem: How does the writer answer the staff?
options: Other local gyms open at six
items.rationale: The writer replies to the staff objection by pointing to two other gyms in town that already open at six.

script: The company wants everyone back in the office five days a week. I understand the reason: it is easier to train new staff when people sit together. But the office only has forty desks and we are fifty-two people. Last month, on the two days when nearly everyone came in, six of us worked in the corridor. If the rule starts in September, that will happen every day. I am not arguing against coming in. I am arguing that three days works and five does not, until there are enough desks.

items.stem: What is the writer's main point?
options: The office is too small for the rule
items.rationale: The writer accepts the reason for coming in and objects that forty desks cannot seat fifty-two people.

items.stem: What does the writer accept about the company's reason?
options: Costs are lower in the office
items.rationale: The second sentence concedes that training new staff is easier when people sit together.

items.stem: What happened last month?
options: Six people worked in the corridor
items.rationale: On the two days when nearly everyone came in, six people had to work in the corridor.

items.stem: What does the writer propose?
options: Three days until desks are added
items.rationale: The final sentence argues that three days works and five does not until there are enough desks.

script: People say that reading reviews before you buy something saves money. I used to think so too. Then I counted. Over three months I read reviews for eleven things and bought nine of them. Without the reviews I would probably have bought four. The reviews did not stop me spending; they made me confident enough to spend. They are useful for choosing between two products. They are not useful for deciding whether to buy at all, and that is the decision that costs money.

items.stem: What did the writer discover?
options: Reviews took too long to read
items.rationale: He read reviews for eleven items and bought nine, where he thinks he would otherwise have bought four.

items.stem: What are reviews good for, according to the writer?
items.rationale: The writer says reviews are useful for choosing between two products but not for deciding whether to buy at all.

items.stem: How long did the writer count for?
items.rationale: The passage says he counted over three months.

items.stem: What does the writer say is the expensive decision?
options: How much to spend on delivery
items.rationale: The last sentence names the decision whether to buy at all as the one that costs money.

script: Our building wants to put a camera at the front door. The reason given is the parcels that went missing in June. I would like the parcels back too, but a camera films everyone who comes and goes, not only the person who took them. Four of the eight flats have already said they are uncomfortable with that. A locked parcel box costs about the same and only records that a box was opened. I would rather try the box first and keep the camera as the answer if the box fails.

items.stem: What does the writer prefer?
items.rationale: The writer proposes trying the parcel box first and keeping the camera as a later option.

items.stem: What is the writer's objection to the camera?
options: It would not have caught the thief
items.rationale: The objection is that a camera films everyone coming and going, not only the person who took the parcels.

items.stem: How many flats object to the camera?
items.rationale: The passage says four of the eight flats are uncomfortable with it.

items.stem: What does the writer say about the cost?
options: The two options cost about the same
items.rationale: The writer states that a locked parcel box costs about the same as the camera.

script: The council is thinking of closing the small library on Mill Road and moving its books to the central one. On paper this makes sense: the central library is bigger and opens longer. But the people who use Mill Road are mostly older, and the bus from that side of town to the centre takes thirty-five minutes and does not run on Sundays. A library you cannot reach is not a library you have. If the council must save money, shorter hours at Mill Road would cost the users far less than closing it.

items.stem: What is the writer against?
items.rationale: The writer argues against closing Mill Road and moving its books to the central library.

items.stem: Why is the central library difficult for Mill Road users?
options: The journey is long and limited
items.rationale: The bus takes thirty-five minutes and does not run on Sundays, and the users are mostly older.

items.stem: What does the writer suggest instead?
items.rationale: The final sentence proposes shorter hours at Mill Road as the cheaper cost to users.

items.stem: What does the writer accept about the council's plan?
options: The central library is bigger and open longer
items.rationale: The writer concedes that on paper the plan makes sense because the central library is bigger and opens longer.

script: Every few years someone proposes that our town should charge for parking in the market square, and every few years the shopkeepers stop it. Their argument is that customers will drive to the retail park instead, where parking is free. I think the argument is weaker than it looks. The square holds sixty cars. On a Saturday morning those sixty spaces are taken by about seventy cars across the whole morning, because people park and stay for hours. A charge of two dollars an hour would not empty the square; it would turn it over. If each space were used by three cars instead of one, the same shops would see three times as many customers. The shopkeepers are defending the parking of people who are already there, and calling it the defence of trade. What they should be asking is who is not coming because there is nowhere to stop.

items.stem: What do the shopkeepers argue?
options: Customers would go to the retail park
items.rationale: Their stated argument is that customers would drive instead to the retail park, where parking is free.

items.stem: What does the writer say a charge would do?
items.rationale: The writer argues a charge would not empty the square but would turn the spaces over.

items.stem: How many cars use the square on a Saturday morning?
items.rationale: The passage says the sixty spaces are taken by about seventy cars across the whole morning.

items.stem: What does the writer accuse the shopkeepers of?
items.rationale: The writer says they are defending the parking of people already there and calling it a defence of trade.

script: A lot of workplaces have replaced the annual review with short monthly conversations, and the change is usually described as kinder. In my experience it is kinder only if the manager was already good at it. The annual review had one thing going for it: it was written down, and both people knew when it was coming. A monthly conversation that happens in a corridor leaves no record, and when a promotion is decided in June nobody can point to what was agreed in March. I am not asking for the old form back. I am asking that whatever replaces it produces a sentence that both people have read. Without that, feedback becomes a matter of who remembers the conversation better, and that is almost never the junior person.

items.stem: What is the writer's main concern about monthly conversations?
items.rationale: The objection is that a corridor conversation leaves no record, so nothing can be pointed to later.

items.stem: What advantage does the writer see in the annual review?
options: It was run by senior staff
items.rationale: The writer says the annual review was written down and both people knew when it was coming.

items.stem: What does the writer ask for?
options: A record both people have read
items.rationale: The writer explicitly does not want the old form back, but wants a sentence both people have read.

items.stem: Who does the writer say loses without a record?
items.rationale: The final sentence says the person who remembers the conversation better is almost never the junior one.

script: There is a common piece of advice that you should always take the job with the higher salary early in your career, because later salaries are calculated from it. The arithmetic is sound and the advice is still wrong more often than people admit. A salary compounds only if you stay long enough to be raised from it, and the higher-paying job in these comparisons is usually the one with the longer hours and the shorter average tenure. If you leave after fourteen months, you carry the title, not the number. What actually compounds is the work you can point to. I have watched two colleagues make opposite choices in the same month. The one who took eight thousand less spent two years on a project that is now on every version of her CV, and she passed the other in salary within four years. That is one comparison and proves nothing on its own; it is only a reason to distrust a rule that sounds like arithmetic but is really a bet about how long you will stay.

items.stem: What does the writer say about the salary advice?
options: Its arithmetic hides a bet about tenure
It applies only to senior roles
items.rationale: The writer accepts the arithmetic and argues it assumes you stay long enough to be raised from the higher figure.

items.stem: What does the writer say actually compounds?
options: The work you can point to
items.rationale: The passage states that what compounds is the work you can point to.

items.stem: What happened to the colleague who took less money?
options: She overtook the other within four years
items.rationale: The colleague who took eight thousand less passed the other in salary within four years.

items.stem: How does the writer describe his own example?
options: One case that proves nothing alone
items.rationale: He says it is one comparison and proves nothing on its own, offering it only as a reason to distrust the rule.

script: Our sports club is deciding whether to spend its reserve on floodlights or on a second changing room. The floodlights would let the senior team train after dark, which is four months of the year. The changing room would let two teams use the pitch on the same afternoon, which is every week. The committee is leaning towards the lights because they are visible, and because a photograph of a lit pitch looks like progress. I would rather we bought the thing nobody photographs. Last season we turned away a junior team because there was nowhere for them to change, and that is a member we lost, not an inconvenience. Lights extend the day for the people who are already here. A changing room lets someone else in.

items.stem: What does the writer prefer the club to buy?
items.rationale: The writer argues for the changing room, describing it as the thing nobody photographs.

items.stem: Why does the committee prefer the lights?
options: They are visible and look like progress
items.rationale: The passage says the committee leans towards lights because they are visible and a photograph of a lit pitch looks like progress.

items.stem: What happened last season?
options: A junior team was turned away
items.rationale: The club turned away a junior team because there was nowhere for them to change.

items.stem: What is the writer's distinction between the two options?
options: One extends the day, the other admits new people
One is cheaper than the other
One is temporary, the other permanent
One helps juniors, the other seniors
items.rationale: The closing sentences contrast lights extending the day for existing members with a changing room letting someone else in.
